title: You branched off the wrong branch. Transplant your work.
summary: Your feature sits on top of a colleague's unmerged branch. Move just your three commits onto main, leaving theirs behind, with rebase --onto.
mental_model: `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>` reads as: take the commits in `upstream..branch`, and replay them on `newbase`. The plain two-argument form is just this with newbase and upstream being the same thing.

steps.title: See the problem
steps.why: Your three commits sit on top of two of your colleague's, which are not going to be merged for weeks. Open a pull request now and it shows five commits and their refactor.
steps.expect: Five commits between main and your branch — only three are yours.

steps.title: Name the range you want to move
steps.why: `colleague/refactor..feature/mine` is exactly your three commits. Getting this range right is the whole job; the rebase itself is mechanical.

verify.label: the range names only your commits

steps.title: Transplant them onto main
steps.why: Read it as: new base is main, take everything after colleague/refactor up to feature/mine, replay it there. The colleague's two commits are simply not in the range, so they stay behind.
steps.expect: Your three commits now sit directly on main's readme commit.

verify.label: the branch is now three commits ahead of main

steps.title: Confirm what came and what did not
steps.why: core.py is gone from your branch entirely; your dosing files are all present. The pull request now shows three commits and one concern.

verify.label: the colleague's refactor did not come along

steps.title: Note that every sha changed
steps.why: Replaying a commit onto a different parent produces a different commit object. The content is identical, the identity is not — which is why rebasing shared branches causes pain.
steps.expect: The reflog shows the pre-rebase positions, with different shas.

steps.title: The two-argument form is the same thing
steps.why: `git rebase main` means `--onto main main HEAD`. Once you see that, the three-argument form stops looking exotic — it is the general case and the short form is the special one.

steps.title: Drop commits from the middle instead
steps.why: `--onto` can also cut commits out: `git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~2` replays the last two commits onto a base three back, discarding the one in between. Same mechanism, different range.

verify.label: your three commits now sit directly on main
the colleague's unmerged refactor was left behind
all of your own work came across
the colleague's branch is untouched — you moved a copy, not their commits

pitfalls: The argument order is newbase, upstream, branch — and the middle one is the commit *before* the first one you want to move. Off-by-one here silently drops or duplicates a commit.
Always check `git log --oneline <upstream>..<branch>` before rebasing. If that list is not exactly what you want to move, the rebase will not be either.
Every replayed commit gets a new sha. If the branch was pushed, you need `--force-with-lease` and a word with anyone who pulled it.
`git rebase --abort` works at any point mid-rebase and restores the original branch exactly.
cheatsheet: drop the commit in the middle
restore the branch as it was
find the pre-rebase tip if you need to start over
